subject: ophthalmology
title: Aqueous Outflow and Canal of Schlemm

steps.tx: **Aqueous outflow** drains the anterior chamber angle through trabecular meshwork into canal of Schlemm, then collector channels to episcleral veins, the conventional route carrying most aqueous. A smaller uveoscleral route passes through ciliary muscle to suprachoroidal space, increased by prostaglandin glaucoma drugs. Intraocular pressure is production divided by outflow ease, so most glaucoma is outflow resistance disease, not overproduction.
steps.say: Trabecular drainage toward episcleral veins carries most aqueous through the conventional route. The smaller uveoscleral route gives prostaglandin responsive drainage through ciliary muscle. Intraocular pressure therefore reflects outflow resistance mainly in glaucoma.

vis.alt: Anterior chamber angle diagram showing aqueous passing through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm canal, and the smaller uveoscleral route through the ciliary muscle.
vis.caption: Most aqueous leaves by the trabecular route into episcleral veins, while a smaller share escapes through the ciliary muscle into the suprachoroidal space. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **canal of Schlemm** is an endothelial lined circular channel in scleral sulcus external to trabecular meshwork, receiving aqueous through inner wall pores and vacuoles before collector channels. It behaves partly like a lymphatic vessel developmentally and collapses when pressure dynamics reverse pathologically. Gonioscopy cannot see the canal directly, only the trabecular pigment above it, so outflow assessment is functional by pressure response.
steps.say: A circular scleral channel gives continuous aqueous reception through inner wall pores and vacuoles. Gonioscopy gives a view of trabecular pigment rather than the canal itself directly. Outflow assessment is therefore functional through pressure response.

steps.tx: **Gonioscopy** places a mirrored contact lens on the anaesthetised cornea to see the drainage angle that the iris otherwise hides. In an open angle the observer identifies Schwalbe line, pigmented trabecular meshwork and the scleral spur in sequence. The canal of Schlemm itself may show as a faint line, sometimes holding a trickle of blood when episcleral pressure rises. Grading this view separates open angle glaucoma from closure.
steps.say: A circular scleral channel gives continuous aqueous reception through inner wall pores. Gonioscopy gives a view of trabecular pigment rather than the canal itself directly.

vis.alt: Gonioscopy view through a contact lens onto an open anterior chamber angle, with trabecular meshwork and the canal of Schlemm labelled in the accompanying section.
vis.caption: The gonioscopy mirror reveals angle structures in sequence, and a wide open angle with visible meshwork excludes closure as the pressure mechanism. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Trabecular meshwork layers filter progressively: uveal, corneoscleral and juxtacanalicular tissue where most resistance resides next to Schlemm inner wall. Ageing, steroid response and pigment or pseudoexfoliation debris raise juxtacanalicular resistance in open angle glaucoma varieties. **Selective laser trabeculoplasty** treats this meshwork biologically without incision, explaining its first line role in modern open angle care.
steps.say: Juxtacanalicular tissue gives most outflow resistance in the trabecular meshwork anatomically. Debris accumulation and steroid response give raised resistance in open angle varieties. Laser treatment gives meshwork targeting without any incision.

steps.tx: Angle anatomy by gonioscopy grades openness from wide ciliary body visibility to closed iris apposition, Shaffer grading detailed in the glaucoma batch. Structures seen in open angle from iris root outward are ciliary body band, scleral spur, trabecular meshwork and Schwalbe line. **Scleral spur** is the white landmark separating ciliary band from meshwork that gonioscopists anchor orientation upon.
steps.say: Gonioscopy grades angle openness by the visible structures seen in sequence. The scleral spur separates ciliary band from trabecular meshwork as a landmark. Orientation during gonioscopy anchors on spur identification first.

steps.tx: Pupillary block closes the angle when iris bombe pushes peripheral iris onto meshwork, relieved by laser iridotomy that equalises chamber pressures. Plateau iris closes by anterior ciliary processes despite patent iridotomy, needing iridoplasty or lens based strategies. **Mechanism first** gonioscopy and imaging therefore precede laser choice, because identical pressure spikes arise from opposite anatomies demanding opposite procedures.
steps.say: Pupillary block needs laser iridotomy while plateau iris needs entirely different strategies. Mechanism assessment is therefore required before laser choice in every angle closure case. Opposite anatomies give identical pressure spikes at presentation.

steps.tx: Episcleral venous pressure sets the floor below which trabecular outflow cannot lower pressure, explaining raised pressure with dilated episcleral vessels in carotid fistula or thyroid orbit disease. Goldmann equation teaching compresses this: pressure equals aqueous flow over outflow facility plus venous pressure. **Venous pressure** elevation therefore mimics outflow block while meshwork remains innocent anatomically.
steps.say: Episcleral venous pressure sets the floor for pressure lowering through the trabecular route. Dilated episcleral vessels therefore indicate venous driven pressure elevation at examination. The meshwork itself remains innocent in venous cases.

steps.tx: Surgical outflow enhancement escalates from laser trabeculoplasty through minimally invasive canal procedures to trabeculectomy filtration and drainage tubes covered in glaucoma lessons. Each step trades efficacy against hypotony and failure risk at a lower target pressure. **Target pressure** individualised by damage severity decides the step, not pressure number alone, linking anatomy to the glaucoma batch directly.
steps.say: Outflow surgery escalates together from laser treatment through to filtration by target need. Damage severity individualises the target pressure decision for each patient. Anatomy therefore links directly to glaucoma management planning.

steps.tx: Developmental angle anomalies block outflow in congenital glaucoma where trabeculodysgenesis prevents drainage despite clear cornea initially, then corneal oedema and enlargement follow pressure. Goniotomy incises the anomalous tissue from inside under gonioscopic view in infants. **Buphthalmos** teaches that infant sclera stretches under pressure unlike adult sclera, enlarging the whole globe as a pressure sign.
steps.say: Developmental angle block gives raised infant pressure while corneal enlargement follows progressively. Infant sclera gives buphthalmos by stretching unlike the rigid adult globe. Goniotomy gives internal incision of the anomalous tissue in infants.

steps.tx: Outflow summary is route, resistance and venous floor. Conventional route dominates, juxtacanalicular tissue resists, Schlemm canal collects, episcleral veins floor the system. Gonioscopy grades access, laser treats meshwork, iridotomy treats block and pressure targets individualise by nerve damage. **Production suppression** is the pharmacological counterweight when outflow cannot be restored sufficiently.
steps.say: Route, resistance and venous floor together give complete organisation of outflow anatomy for examinations. Gonioscopy gives access grading while treatments follow the mechanism found. Production suppression gives a counterweight to outflow that cannot be restored.
